name: Friction-maxxing

card.summary: A 2026 self-improvement term for deliberately choosing small everyday inconveniences, such as cooking from a cookbook or paying cash, to build effort tolerance and resilience that proponents tie to sticking with self-improvement routines.
card.note: A lifestyle idea rather than an appearance technique; no studies use the term.

quick.overview:
Friction-maxxing is a term that encourages people to seek out everyday inconvenience on purpose, as a counterweight to technology that removes effort. It was popularised by Kathryn Jezer-Morton's January 2026 article in New York Magazine's The Cut, according to Grokipedia.

Its link to looks is through habits: proponents describe it as building tolerance for effort and discomfort, which in the -maxxing vocabulary is the same capacity that consistent training, skincare and grooming routines draw on.
quick.how: Examples attributed to the idea include using a physical cookbook instead of an AI assistant, paying with cash and switching to a flip phone. Practitioners adopt these as small, deliberate choices rather than a structured program, and there is no standard method or timeline.
quick.risks: No health risks are documented. Commentators quoted in coverage questioned its practicality in daily life, according to Grokipedia.

lead: Friction-maxxing is a cultural idea that encourages people to deliberately embrace everyday inconvenience as a response to digital technologies that automate and simplify life.[1] Grokipedia says it was popularised by the article "In 2026, We Are Friction-Maxxing" by Kathryn Jezer-Morton in The Cut, published January 3, 2026, as a proposed New Year's resolution.[1]

The term uses the -maxxing suffix from looksmaxxing and related self-improvement vocabulary. Proponents frame building tolerance for friction as a way to build resilience and presence; how it connects to appearance is through that effort tolerance, for example sticking with training or care routines, rather than any direct effect on features.[1]

Examples cited include replacing AI assistants with physical cookbooks, paying with cash and using a flip phone.[1] Grokipedia reports early coverage in The Guardian, and mixed reader responses ranging from enthusiasm to skepticism about practicality.[1] No studies use the term.

chain: Supports consistency in other routines, including appearance routines
angle.text: The idea is that practising small inconveniences makes effort feel normal, which proponents link to resilience. People applying the -maxxing frame to looks would connect that to keeping up training and grooming habits.

paras: Friction-maxxing advocates intentionally cultivating tolerance for everyday inconveniences to counteract the passivity fostered by effortless digital interfaces; the article's argument is that technologies selling escapism leave people less able to handle ordinary friction.[1]
Grokipedia reports that the term originated in the January 2026 article and that The Guardian covered it by January 6.[1] These details come from an AI-generated page and are unverified.
Reactions to the article are described as ranging from enthusiasm for its anti-technology stance to skepticism about its practicality.[1]

timeline.event: Kathryn Jezer-Morton publishes "In 2026, We Are Friction-Maxxing" in The Cut.[1]
